L30@P2: Abstract
L31@P2: We study potential drivers for a large cross section of commodity futures. Unlike previous
L32@P2: studies, we examine the effect of monthly drivers on daily returns using mixed-frequency
L33@P2: Granger causality tests. We find real economic activity as a main driver on a monthly basis,
L34@P2: whereas financial variables seem to affect returns at daily frequency. The linkages are timevarying for various stages of the financialization of commodity markets with an overall
L35@P2: dissipating impact in the recent period of de-financialization. As our results strongly differ
L36@P2: from traditional low-frequency Granger causality tests under the temporal aggregation of
L37@P2: futures returns, we show the economic value of accessing information at a higher frequency
L38@P2: in an out-of-sample trading study. Our findings emphasize the importance of using mixedfrequency techniques to uncover relationships between monthly-published macroeconomic
L39@P2: variables and commodity prices.
L40@P2: Keywords: Commodity futures, VAR, Granger causality, Mixed data sampling
L41@P2: JEL classification: C58; G17; Q02

L54@P3: 1. Introduction
L55@P3: Since it is well established that prices of various “unrelated” commodities tend to
L56@P3: co-move, researchers are trying to understand the driving forces behind joint fluctuations
L57@P3: in commodity prices.1 Uncovering the effects that influence the cross-section of commodity futures fosters the accuracy of market research outlooks and helps commercial
L58@P3: traders to improve their hedging decisions. As correlations among commodities intensifiedduring the so-called“financialization” of commodity futuresmarkets (Tang&Xiong,
L59@P3: 2012; Büyükşahin & Robe, 2014; Bhardwaj et al., 2016), it is also crucial for financial
L60@P3: investors to understand the drivers shared bymultiple commodities to assess the level of
L61@P3: diversification in their portfolios properly.
L62@P3: The existing literature attributes the presence of commonalities in commodity prices
L63@P3: to three major factors. Firstly, commodity prices react to changes in macroeconomic
L64@P3: fundamentals that shift aggregate supply and demand or its expectations (Pindyck &
L65@P3: Rotemberg, 1990).Thesefundamentals includereal economic activityorexchange rates,
L66@P3: for instance.2 Secondly, a high portion of the co-movement can be attributed to the
L67@P3: financialization of commodity markets. With financialization, commodities became a
L68@P3: new investable asset class in the eyes of financial investors. For example, Tang & Xiong
L69@P3: (2012) ascribe the tighter link between different commodity markets to the trading of
L70@P3: commodity index investors as they observe stronger effects for index compared with offindex commodities.3 Results of Adams et al. (2020) indicate a growing importance of
L71@P3: financial variables in explaining commodity returns during financialization, which is of
L72@P3: significant interest to our study. Lastly, various uncertainty measures have been found
L73@P3: to affect commodity prices (e.g. Joëts et al., 2017). Effects originating from uncertainty
L74@P3: 1See, e.g., Pindyck & Rotemberg (1990); Tang & Xiong (2012); Byrne et al. (2013); Chen et al. (2014);
L75@P3: West & Wong (2014); Gao & Süss (2015); Ohashi & Okimoto (2016); Le Pen & Sévi (2018); Delle Chiaie
L76@P3: et al. (2022), among others.
L77@P3: 2The effect of real economic activity is documented in Pindyck & Rotemberg 1990; West & Wong 2014;
L78@P3: Delle Chiaie et al. 2022, while the impact of changes in the US-Dollar exchange rate is documented in
L79@P3: Chen et al. 2014; West & Wong 2014, amongst others. We provide a more detailed review on potential
L80@P3: drivers of commodity prices and related empirical findings of the literature in Section 3.
L81@P3: 3Academic literature on causes of financialization and the motivation of financial investors seeking, e.g.,
L82@P3: portfolio diversification is becoming increasingly ample (Tang & Xiong, 2012; Cheng & Xiong, 2014;
L83@P3-4: Adams & Glück, 2015; Gao & Süss, 2015; Ohashi & Okimoto, 2016; Le Pen & Sévi, 2018).3
L84@P4: affect commodity markets both through fundamental and financial channels.
L85@P4: The majority of the existing literature on the drivers of commodity prices and their
L86@P4: co-movement uses temporally aggregated monthly, quarterly, or even annual returns for
L87@P4: empirical analyses as most macroeconomic indicators are available at amonthly or lower
L88@P4: frequency. Thisaggregationresults inthelossof valuableinformationinherentinhigherfrequency data and can distort empirical findings (Marcellino, 1999).4 The few studies
L89@P4: using higher-frequency data restrict themselves to a small set of potential drivers (e.g.
L90@P4: Gao & Süss, 2015; Andreasson et al., 2016), which, in turn, leads to ignoring important
L91@P4: variable available only at monthly data frequency.
L92@P4: Unlikeprevious studies,weseek to identify “commondrivers” thatjointly affect commodity futures returns by employing mixed-frequency (MF) Granger causality (Ghysels
L93@P4: et al.,2016). Themethodallows to study the relationoflower-frequent, suchasmonthlyavailablefundamental,financial, anduncertainty-relatedvariables,tovariables available
L94@P4: at a higher data frequency, such as daily or weekly commodity futures returns. Thereby,
L95@P4: we circumvent the aforementioned difficulties caused by temporal aggregation or variable
L96@P4: omittance. We do not aim to determine commodity-specific drivers as in Kang et al.
L97@P4: (2020),nordoweexplicitly focusonidentifyingdrivers of a commoncomponentincommodity prices like Byrne et al. (2013), for instance. Instead, we argue that if a single
L98@P4: factor significantly affects individual futures returns across different types of commodities, it should also constitute a cause behind their co-movement.
L99@P4: Wefindthatmostcommodityfutures returnsaredrivenmainlybychanges inrealeconomic activity on a monthly basis, whereas financial variables affect price movements on
L100@P4: a daily level. Many futures returns are also influenced by uncertainty, both in the shortand long-term, depending on the cause of uncertainty. We further show that the relations between commodities and drivers are time-varying throughout the distinct stages of
L101@P4: financialization (Natoli, 2021). Our results indicate that not only linkages from financial
L102@P4: but also from fundamental and uncertainty variables to the broad range of commodity
L103@P4: 4Ghysels et al.(2016), forinstance, points outthattemporal aggregation can cause both spurious causality
L104@P4-5: and spurious non-causality.4
L105@P5: futures dissolved in the recent period of the so-called “de-financialization” (2014 onward).
L106@P5: Additionally,we find thattemporally aggregating commodity returns—as is done in previous work—leads to different, potentially erroneous conclusions in the Granger causality
L107@P5: analysis underpinning Ghysels et al. (2016) and Bevilacqua et al. (2019). With an outof-sample trading study,wedemonstrate that MFmodels improve the economic valueof
L108@P5: directional returnpredictionsovertraditionalmodelsestimatedfrommonthlydataonly.
L109@P5: Our contribution to the literature on commodity futures is twofold. Firstly, we add to
L110@P5: the literature on co-movement byproviding further evidence on common return drivers
L111@P5: of commodity futures using a novel MF approach. Secondly, we show the time-variation
L112@P5: inthe relationof commodity futures to their returndrivers overdisparate stages ofthe financialization. Particularly little evidence exists for the period of de-financialization since
L113@P5: samples of most studies end before 2014. We also contribute to the literature on Mixed
L114@P5: Data Sampling (MIDAS) by showing the economic benefit of utilizing higher-frequency
L115@P5: data to uncover relationships between macroeconomic indicators and commodity futures.
L116@P5: The remainder ofthepaper isorganizedas follows. Wedescribeourmethodology and
L117@P5: data in Section 2 and 3. Section 4 presents our empirical results. Section 5 concludes.
L118@P5: 2. Methodology
L119@P5: We build our testing framework on the recently proposed MF Granger causality test
L120@P5: (Ghysels et al., 2016) based on MF Vector Autoregression (MF-VAR Ghysels, 2016). In
L121@P5: contrast to traditional VAR models that can be estimated only from variables that share
L122@P5: the same data frequency, MF-VARs combine information of multiple time series at distinct
L123@P5: sampling frequencies. Hence,whenanalyzing thenexus oflow-frequency (LF) andhighfrequency (HF) processes, data from the HF process does not need to be temporally
L124@P5: aggregated to the common lower frequency. While most other MIDAS models are used
L125@P5: for predicting LF time series with HF information, MF-VARs also allow to study the
L126@P5: oppositedirection, e.g.,testing forGranger causality fromLFmacroeconomic indicators
L127@P5: to HF commodity futures returns. Moreover, recent findings by Foroni et al. (2018)
L128@P5-6: suggest that LF information can be useful for HF variables in a MIDAS framework.5

L316@P10: 3.1. Commodity futures
L317@P10: Our data set covers a wide range of agricultural and energy commodities as well as
L318@P10: industrialandpreciousmetals. Webuildour studybasedonfutures fortworeasons. First,
L319@P10: because they are traded on exchanges,their prices are more transparentthan spot prices
L320@P10: and may also contain more information due to their higher trading volume. Second,
L321@P10: it enables us to test the economic significance of our results in a subsequent trading
L322@P10: application. Table1presents summary statistics fordaily log returns. These daily returns
L323@P10: will serve as inputfor VARmodels,thatinclude daily-available driver variables. Tocheck
L324@P10: the robustness of our results, we also construct equally-weighted commodity portfolios
L325@P10: and extract a common factor in the returns defined as the first principal component of
L326@P10: standardized log returns of all 32 commodities, for which data is available over the full
L327@P10: time period. Figure 1 depicts how the returns of different types of commodities and
L328@P10: the common return factor evolve throughout our sample. The co-movement becomes
L329@P10: particularly clear with simultaneous surging prices of raw materials starting from the
L330@P10: early 2000s followed by jointly crashing prices during the Global Financial Crisis, which
L331@P10: is also captured by the common component and found in extant literature (e.g., Ohashi
